corpus.title: Trump administration sanctions International Criminal Court
corpus.signal_text:
Trump administration sanctions International Criminal Court
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The United States has announced sweeping sanctions against the International Criminal Court (ICC), escalating Trump’s war on the international tribunal.
“We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate,” US secretary of state Marco Rubio said in an announcement.
The Trump administration has previously pledged to dismantle the court “brick by brick” and has sanctioned 13 current and former staff members, but this is the first time it has levied sanctions against the institution itself.
Ahead of the announcement, prime minister Rob Jetten said the Netherlands will protect the ICC “stone by stone”.
Foreign minister Tom Berendsen said the country would stand behind the court. “The announced sanctions against the International Criminal Court are an undesirable new escalation,” Berendsen said in a statement. “I deeply regret this new step.”
The sanctions will cut the court off from any US company or organisation, including providers of financial and technology services.
The announcement came hours after South African jurist Navi Pillay, who has served as a judge at both the ICC and the International Court of Justice in The Hague, was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize.
Trump has long coveted the prize, telling reporters earlier this week that he deserved the award for what he said was ending eight wars.

The United States announcement of new sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC), hours after the Nobel Peace Prize went to one of its former judges Navi Pillay, has provoked widespread international criticism.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington would ban transactions with what he called a "rogue court".
"Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC," he added.
European nations and the United Nations have led the opposition, while Israel has welcomed Washington's decision.
Here are key reactions:
'Serious blow': UN
UN chief Antonio Guterres condemned the US decision, saying he was "deeply alarmed by the expected impact" of the measures, a spokesman said.
"Today's decision marks a serious blow to our collective pursuit of international criminal justice, of which the ICC is a key pillar," spokesman Stephane Dujarric told reporters.
"The secretary-general reiterates his unwavering support for the independence of the court and its officials."
UN human rights chief Volker Turk said the sanctions, "the latest in a series of retaliatory steps against the ICC and its personnel... are unacceptable".
Netanyahu support
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu praised the US sanctions, a rare show of support for Washington's action.
"The ICC is not a court," Netanyahu's office posted on X.
"It is a political body that poses a mortal threat to law-abiding democracies worldwide and to the very idea of national sovereignty."

The European Union also described the US sanctions "deeply regrettable".

corpus.title: US imposes sanctions on the International Criminal Court
corpus.signal_text:
Audio By Vocalize
The United States on Friday announced sanctions on the International Criminal Court, vowing to cripple the tribunal's operations just hours after the Nobel Peace Prize went to a former ICC judge who warned of mounting political attacks on the court.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington would ban transactions with what he called a "rogue court," escalating a long-running campaign by President Donald Trump's administration against the Hague-based tribunal.
"Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC," Rubio said in a statement.
But the immediate impact of the sanctions was softened by a series of exemptions that offer a de facto six-month grace period.
The State Department said that was meant to give the court's member states time to show "meaningful progress" toward addressing US concerns.
The grace period could be adjusted depending on the "success or failure" of those efforts, the department added.
The court rejected the US sanctions as an attack on international law and warned in a statement that "history will judge this moment."
Countries including Canada, France, Germany, Japan and the United Kingdom said in a joint statement that they "strongly disagree" with the announcement.
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres called the US decision "a serious blow to our collective pursuit of international criminal justice, of which the ICC is a key pillar."
The European Union called the sanctions "deeply regrettable" and said it was "ready to take any necessary measures to enable the court to carry out its work."
The European Commission, the EU's executive arm, said it hoped the six-month delay meant "there is room for dialogue."
Rights group Amnesty International urged countries to "resist" the move, saying the sanctions were "designed to isolate and ultimately destroy" the court.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who faces an ICC arrest warrant over alleged crimes in Gaza, praised the US action.
"The ICC is not a court. It is a political body that poses a mortal threat to law-abiding democracies worldwide and to the very idea of national sovereignty," his office posted on X.

corpus.title: US vows to ‘cripple ICC’ as former judge Navi Pillay wins Nobel Peace Prize
corpus.signal_text:
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced new sanctions on the International Criminal Court on Friday, just hours after former ICC judge Navi Pillay of South Africa won the Nobel Peace Prize.
“President [Donald] Trump will never allow the International Criminal Court to prosecute Americans,” Rubio said in a video statement. “That is why, today, the United States is sanctioning the International Criminal Court. We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate.”
ICC Deputy Prosecutor Nazhat Shameem Khan told Reuters the sanctions “must be condemned” and vowed that the court would fight on. “The sanctions are intended to undermine the rule of law internationally and the work that an independent judicial institution is doing,” Khan said.
The new sanctions mark a significant escalation in the Trump administration’s fight to undermine a global body that has infuriated the US by issuing arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former defence minister Yoav Gallant and investigating alleged war crimes by US service members in Afghanistan. Pillay chaired the UN Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory that concluded last year that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza.
Neither the US nor Israel are a party to the Rome Statute that established the ICC.
International campaign to dismantle ICC
The second Trump administration first announced visa restrictions and financial penalties for people who help the ICC investigate US citizens and US allies in February 2025. Since then, the US has sanctioned more than a dozen judges and other court officials.
In July, Rubio launched an international campaign to dismantle the court, calling it a threat to US sovereignty. “Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC. We expect our allies, many of whom are part of the ICC and that rely on American servicemembers for their defence, to rein in the court,” Rubio said. “If they do not, the US will continue its campaign to dismantle the ICC, brick by brick, until Americans are threatened no longer.”
The pressure campaign has had some effect. The authoritarian states of Chad and Venezuela withdrew in late July, with Chadian Foreign Minister Abdoulaye Sabre Fadoul citing US pressure.
